summary: Updates RFC 4271 to forbid using Autonomous System number 0 in BGP OPEN messages and in AS_PATH, AS4_PATH, AGGREGATOR and AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes of UPDATE messages.

plainLanguage.summary: House number zero is not allowed on the street. Routers should reject messages that use it.

questions: what happens when bgp receives as 0
subtitle: BGP routers must never originate, propagate or accept AS number 0.

tldr.problem: No BGP specification clearly said AS 0 was forbidden, yet a ROA listing AS 0 as the only origin is used to say a prefix must not be routed.
tldr.mechanism: A BGP speaker MUST NOT originate or propagate AS 0, UPDATEs carrying it are treated as malformed, and an OPEN claiming AS 0 is rejected.
tldr.outcome: Routes containing AS 0 are ignored everywhere, which stops anyone from hijacking address space that its holder marked as not in use.

today: RFC 7607 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4271. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why AS 0 Needed a Rule
sections.content:
AS 0 was listed in the IANA registry as reserved and usable to identify non-routed networks. RFC 6491 says that AS 0 in a Route Origin Attestation (ROA) marks a prefix and its more specifics as not to be used in routing, which lets a resource holder signal that a prefix should not be routed.

To respond to that signal, BGP implementations must not accept or propagate routes containing AS 0. The RFC says no clear statement proscribing AS 0 existed in any BGP specification. It fixes that omission, most importantly for the AS_PATH, and codifies what at least two implementations already do: discard such routes. It updates the error handling in Sections 6.2 and 6.3 of RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: An owner can say "nobody should use this address" by naming zero as its only user. For that to work, routers must refuse anything that mentions zero.

sections.title: Required BGP Behavior
sections.content:
A BGP speaker MUST NOT originate or propagate a route with AS number zero in the AS_PATH, AS4_PATH, AGGREGATOR or AS4_AGGREGATOR attributes.

  • An UPDATE with AS 0 in AS_PATH or AGGREGATOR MUST be considered malformed and handled under RFC 7606.
  • An UPDATE with AS 0 in AS4_PATH or AS4_AGGREGATOR MUST be considered malformed and handled under RFC 6793.
  • If a speaker receives zero as the peer AS in an OPEN message, it MUST abort the connection and send a NOTIFICATION with Error Code "OPEN Message Error" and subcode "Bad Peer AS". A router MUST NOT initiate a connection claiming to be AS 0.

Authors of future extensions that carry an AS number are encouraged to remember AS 0 is reserved and say how to handle it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a message mentions zero, treat it as broken. If a router says its own number is zero, hang up on it.

sections.title: IANA Registry Change
sections.content: IANA updated the registry for 16-bit Autonomous System Numbers so that the entry for AS 0 is simply "Reserved", dropping the earlier wording about identifying non-routed networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list now just says zero is reserved, with no other use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) resource holder can issue a ROA naming AS 0 as the only valid origin, stating that an address resource is not in use. Because every implementation that sees AS 0 in a route ignores that route, a malicious party cannot announce routes containing AS 0 to hijack those resources. Standardizing the behavior for an AS_PATH or AS4_PATH with AS 0 also makes it better defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Since everyone ignores zero, a bad actor cannot use it to sneak into an address that its owner marked as unused.
